Lessons.Title: Rational Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: A rational function is a quotient of polynomials; the original denominator cannot be zero, even where a common factor cancels.
Arrow notation x→a− or x→a+ describes one-sided input behavior. A vertical asymptote often signals diverging output, while a removable discontinuity is a finite-valued hole.
After factoring numerator and denominator, cancel common factors to locate holes but retain original domain exclusions. Remaining real denominator zeros yield vertical asymptotes.

Horizontal asymptotes follow degree comparison: numerator degree lower gives y=0; equal gives the ratio of leading coefficients; higher generally requires polynomial division for polynomial end behavior.
A graph can cross a horizontal asymptote but does not take values at a vertical asymptote's x-coordinate; a hole is an excluded point on the simplified curve.
Use intercepts, limits, sign charts and asymptotes to sketch each branch. Contextual units and positive-domain restrictions are essential in rational models.
Independent Try It 1: For f(x)=−1/(x+4), determine f(x) as x→−4− and x→−4+.
Independent Try It 2: For g(x)=3/(x−1)−2 identify both asymptotes.
Independent Try It 3: A tank holds 30 g in 60 L; add 3 g/min and 2 L/min. Write c(t) and its long-run level.
Independent Try It 4: Find domain of (x−5)/(x²−16).
Independent Try It 5: For (x²−9)/(x−3), locate the hole.
Independent Try It 6: Find end asymptote for (4x²+3)/(x²+1).
Independent Try It 7: Find x/y intercepts of (x+3)/(x−2).
Independent Try It 8: Construct a rational function with zero x=2, vertical asymptote x=−1, horizontal asymptote y=3.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: (1) Analyze f(x)=(x²−4)/(x²+x−6) for its original domain, hole, vertical and horizontal asymptotes. (2) Analyze g(x)=(x−1)²/((x+2)(x−3)) for zeros, poles, multiplicities, horizontal asymptote and y-intercept. (3) A tank contains 5 kg solute in 50 L and receives 1 kg solute and 5 L liquid per minute: write C(t), domain and long-run concentration.

WorkedExamples.Title: Arrow notation
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=1/(x−2), determine behavior as x approaches 2 from each side.
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
WorkedExamples.Check: The denominator changes from negative to positive through zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Transform a reciprocal
WorkedExamples.Question: Graph g(x)=−2/(x+3)+1 and state both asymptotes.
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
WorkedExamples.Check: Apply translation left 3, up 1 and vertical reflection/stretch by 2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rational concentration model
WorkedExamples.Question: A tank has 12 kg solute in 100 L and adds 2 kg/min and 5 L/min. Express the concentration after t minutes and its long-run level.
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
WorkedExamples.Check: Divide total solute mass by total volume; compare leading coefficients.

WorkedExamples.Title: Domain restrictions
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the domain of h(x)=(x+1)/(x²−9).
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
WorkedExamples.Check: Factor denominator (x−3)(x+3); never include zero-denominator points.

WorkedExamples.Title: Vertical asymptotes
WorkedExamples.Question: Find vertical asymptotes of (x+1)/((x−2)(x+4)).
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
WorkedExamples.Check: Neither denominator factor cancels with the numerator.

WorkedExamples.Title: Hole versus asymptote
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=((x−2)(x+3))/((x−2)(x+1)), identify the hole and vertical asymptote.
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Steps: Hole at (2,5/3); vertical asymptote x=−1; domain excludes both 2 and −1.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Hole at (2,5/3); vertical asymptote x=−1; domain excludes both 2 and −1.
WorkedExamples.Check: Cancel only to compute the limit; original function remains undefined at x=2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Slant asymptote
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the end behavior of (x²+2x+3)/(x+1).
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
WorkedExamples.Check: Polynomial division gives the linear quotient and vanishing remainder ratio.

WorkedExamples.Title: Horizontal asymptote
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the horizontal asymptote of (3x²+1)/(2x²+5).
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
WorkedExamples.Check: Equal polynomial degrees: leading coefficient ratio.

WorkedExamples.Title: All vertical and horizontal asymptotes
WorkedExamples.Question: Analyze (x²−1)/(x²−4).
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Steps: Vertical asymptotes x=−2, x=2; horizontal y=1; zeros x=±1.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Vertical asymptotes x=−2, x=2; horizontal y=1; zeros x=±1.
WorkedExamples.Check: Factor numerator and denominator and compare degrees.

WorkedExamples.Title: Intercepts of rational function
WorkedExamples.Question: Find intercepts and asymptotes of (x−4)/(x+2).
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Steps: x-intercept (4,0), y-intercept (0,−2), vertical x=−2, horizontal y=1.
WorkedExamples.Answer: x-intercept (4,0), y-intercept (0,−2), vertical x=−2, horizontal y=1.
WorkedExamples.Check: Numerator zero produces x-intercept only if denominator nonzero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Graph from critical points
WorkedExamples.Question: Sketch f(x)=x/(x²−1) with intercepts and asymptotes.
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
Steps: Intercept (0,0); vertical x=±1; horizontal y=0. On (1,∞) graph is positive, on (0,1) negative.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Intercept (0,0); vertical x=±1; horizontal y=0. On (1,∞) graph is positive, on (0,1) negative.
WorkedExamples.Check: Use signs between critical inputs to place branches.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct a rational function
WorkedExamples.Question: Construct f with simple vertical asymptotes −2 and 3, zero at 1 and y-intercept 1/3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Factor and analyze the original domain, limits, intercepts and end behavior as appropriate.
WorkedExamples.Check: Choose factored numerator/denominator and solve f(0)=1/3 for scale.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rational function and domain
KeyConcepts.Rule: Exclude every zero of the original denominator.

KeyConcepts.Title: Removable hole
KeyConcepts.Definition: A common factor cancels while its root remains excluded from the domain.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Evaluate the simplified expression at the excluded input to find the hole's y-coordinate.

KeyConcepts.Title: Vertical asymptote
KeyConcepts.Definition: A vertical line where the function grows unbounded on at least one side.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check uncancelled real denominator factors and one-sided behavior.

KeyConcepts.Title: Horizontal/slant asymptotes
KeyConcepts.Definition: Lines approached as input grows without bound.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use degree comparisons and long division; horizontal lines may be crossed.

Visuals.Title: Rational behavior by numerator/denominator degree
Visuals.Description: Independent degree classification rather than a copied source illustration.

Rows.Label: degree numerator one higher
Cells: linear slant if quotient has degree 1

SummaryPoints: Original denominator zeros are always excluded.
Cancel common factors to distinguish holes from vertical asymptotes.
A horizontal asymptote can be crossed.
Use intercepts and branch signs in addition to asymptotes.
Context models require units and permissible input ranges.
Cool-down requires factor cancellation without restoring excluded inputs, pole/root multiplicities, and consistent application units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a cancelled factor as an allowed input.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Cancelling does not restore undefined domain values.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep the original denominator restrictions and graph a hole.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming every horizontal asymptote is uncrossable.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Horizontal asymptotes describe end behavior, not forbidden output values.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Solve f(x)=asymptote value and check any finite intersections.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forgetting that a denominator zero may create a hole.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A common numerator factor cancels and leaves finite limit.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Factor first and distinguish cancelled from remaining factors.
